```release-note
kube-scheduler implements scheduling hints for the VolumeRestriction plugin.
The scheduling hints allow the scheduler to only retry scheduling a Pod 
that was previously rejected by the VolumeRestriction plugin in three situations.
a. A new node added.
b. A pod delete, and the deleted pod conflicts with the current pod has readWriteOncePodPVCs.
c. A new pvc added, and the pvc belongs to pod.
```

issue_context.title: [Umbrella] Implement QueueingHintFn in in-tree plugins
issue_context.body:
### What would you like to be added?

In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/118551, we implemented `QueueingHintFn` in `EventsToRegister ` which allows each plugin to filter out useless events to requeue Pod back to the activeQ. (See the PR or [the original proposal](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1S1_OqwCN2oY0Xp4dZt6XLCQQGu7dWm96blgXmGKhwSo/edit#heading=h.xpaj7b9yvnh3) about the details)
Basically, all in-tree plugins, which implements PreFilter or Filter, should have `QueueingHintFn` to achieve the efficient requeueing. 

Please feel free to assign what you'd like to work on. And please comment in this issue before starting to work on so that we can avoid many people from working on the same thing!

- [x] InterPodAffinity @nayihz https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122471
- [x] Dynamic resource @pohly https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119078
- [x] NodeAffinity @carlory https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119155 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122309
- [x] NodePorts @carlory https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119176
- [x] NodeResourceFit  @carlory https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119177
- [x] NodeUnschedulable @wackxu @carlory  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119396 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122334
- [x] CSILimits @utam0k https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121508
- [x] TopologySpread @nayihz https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122195
- [x] TaintToleration  @wackxu @sanposhiho https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119397 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124287
- [x] VolumeBinding @YamasouA @bells17 
- [x] VolumeRestriction @HirazawaUi https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125279 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125280
- [x] VolumeZone @Gekko0114 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119373

/sig scheduling
/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm

### Why is this needed?

It will contribute to the enqueue efficiency a lot and thus overall scheduling performance should get improved significantly by preventing the useless retry on the scheduling as much as possible.

@Huang-Wei and I were discussing the topic of SchedulingHints a little.

The hints seem to be very verbose into all the possibilities that can make a pod schedulable, which can lead to:
- a high maintenance cost
- expensive event handlers, ultimately affecting overall performance

OTOH, we have seen in our fleet that the SchedulingHints framework, without any hints enabled, led to high memory utilization (50% increase for the fleet) and, in big clusters, patterns of memory leaks.

With all of that, it's becoming hard to justify further investments in the feature, at least in its current form.

Listing all positive alternatives:
- Remove the feature (what are we losing?)
- Rework the framework, how events are stored, maybe put caps, and so on.
- Limit the complexity that scheduling hints are allowed to have (for example, disallow querying of multiple objects to make a decision).

(I wanted to discuss this in a SIG meeting, but it's hard due to the timezone difference with @sanposhiho).

FYI @pohly, as I know DRA kind of depends on this feature. But DRA could implement more traditional (non-extensible) event handlers. Question: do scheduling hints matter equally for the semantic model?

> a high maintenance cost

This is.. Yea, especially in this early phase, we've got many PRs, and PRs are waiting for reviews for a long time while our bandwidth is limited. And also we'll have to keep them maintained in the future too.

> expensive event handlers, ultimately affecting overall performance

Any GitHub issue we have? Which performance is it affecting? I couldn't find and don't remember a report of such.

> OTOH, we have seen in our fleet that the SchedulingHints framework, without any hints enabled, lead to high memory utilization (50% increase for the fleet) and, in big clusters, patterns of memory leaks.

We noticed it, and have possible solutions -
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/120622

and... reviews are pending over there too, though.

> Listing all positive alternatives:

So, if the core problem is that we cannot spare any more time on this feature (esp reviews) based on priorities, then the only complete solution would be the removal of the feature, unfortunately. 

Regarding the memory issue (and possibly throughput issue(?) that I haven't grasped yet), there are solutions we haven't yet done, and "Rework the framework, how events are stored" should be considered after them (if they don't solve the issue enough). 

I don't quite understand the last one; any QHints that are too complex actually? If yes, we can loosen the scope of those specific QHints only. I'm not sure we have to have some such limitations entirely.

> FYI @pohly, as I know DRA kind of depends on this feature. But DRA could implement more traditional (non-extensible) event handlers. Question: do scheduling hints matter equally for the semantic model?

They probably matter less because there's less back-and-forth through the apiserver. But there are still some cases where specific pods get put into the unschedulable queue and become schedulable only when specific claims are updated. To give you a full answer I'll have to set up a benchmark in scheduler_perf and do a comparison with and with queuing hints - I'll add this to my TODO list...

What I learned about queueingHint from code reading and reviewing is a) the hint mechanism itself is not that complex (except the inflight pods), thanks to @sanposhiho efforts, but the hintFunc is trivial 2) we do not have a report or test about how hint improves the scheduling throughout although we always said that theoretically it does. 3) queueingHint does solve some problems like `preCheck` and inflight pods 4) We should rework about the memory leakage problem, but actually this is a problem we have now for missing the inflight pods.

TL;DR: I can take over the review work once we reach an agreement. Like whether it's possible to fix the memory problem in prior, how to make the hintFunc simple, IIUC, if we do nothing, we still have the similar performance as we have before.
cc @gabesaba

>> expensive event handlers, ultimately affecting overall performance
>
> Any GitHub issue we have? Which performance is it affecting? I couldn't find and don't remember a report of such.

I didn't see any issue specific to scheduling hints, however @gabesaba just filed #124384, in which calculations from the traditional event handlers hold the lock for too long, dramatically increasing the scheduling latency. Making complex scheduling hints has the potential of running into similar problems.

> We noticed it, and have possible solutions -
> https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/120622
>
> and... reviews are pending over there too, though.

Yes, I acknowledge that, but it's not just about reviews. We don't currently have reproducible scenarios that can tell us if the solution will scale. A reviewer might not be able to see this. I'm hoping we can enhance the scheduler_perf tests, bringing them to the extreme. Without them, it's hard to discern whether a change is good.

> I don't quite understand the last one; any QHints that are too complex actually? If yes, we can loosen the scope of those specific QHints only. I'm not sure we have to have some such limitations entirely.

What I mean is that the code of each of the scheduling hints is quite complex. This means that we could easily leave pods unschedulable if we missed a case or we introduce new filtering behavior and we forget to update the hints accordingly. But also runtime complexity. My proposal would be along the lines of keeping all scheduling hints around 10 lines max, and avoiding loops over lists of objects. Basically, we should be doing O(1) operations on the object update.

Back to reviews.... it comes back to the same complexity point above. If the hint is too complex, it's hard for a reviewer to keep a mental model of all the possible scenarios that could make a pod schedulable, and to be sure that nothing was missed. Maybe we can start with simpler checks that could have false positives, because today almost every event would make a pod go back to the scheduling queue, so it would not be a regression.

After reading all the points from @alculquicondor, 

I said:
> if the core problem is that we cannot spare any more time on this feature (esp reviews) based on priorities, then the only complete solution would be the removal of the feature, unfortunately. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118893#issuecomment-2062867701

But, seems like it's not the case. And, @kerthcet raised a hand for help of reviewing (thanks a lot!), which would improve the situation where we only had me continuously taking the review effort for QHints, and PRs got eventually blocked for the second review.

Regarding two issues (high memory consumption and throughput), definitely we have to work on them, including scheduler_perf improvement to measure it. (all action items are already listed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/120622) 
However, again, we have done literally _nothing_ for those issues; it's too early to say we cannot solve them technically. 

Lastly about the complexity of QHint,

> My proposal would be along the lines of keeping all scheduling hints around 10 lines max, and avoiding loops over lists of objects. Basically, we should be doing O(1) operations on the object update.

I'd agree with having "avoiding loops" policy, which I also believe we can avoid one kind of complexity.

But, disagree with 10 lines max; Regardless of the line length, it should be accepted as long as it's simple enough, which I believe most of the current QHints are. 

I admit https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121508 is very complex and probably we can reduce the scope. 
But, I don't remember other QHints which I feel too complex to be manageable. ...Yes, it's subjective, maybe some other QHints look very complex to some people, so, I asked "which one(s) is too complex" at the first comment. We can reduce the scope of them accordingly so that we can make them simple enough / maintainable.

> But, disagree with 10 lines max;

I just meant it as a general rule of thumb. But I think you got the idea.

Not sure if I would call this one too complex, but it accesses a lister.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5e229a02d34976bf41ad93d2a8ad86ac28ac5f84/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go#L437

In the topic of reviews, I'm trying to make some time to review more PRs, but it's been challenging. I hope to have more time next month.

Yes, let's confirm here that we can reduce the scope if QHint is growing too complex. No need to filter out events finely in all QHints. One criterion is "avoiding loops over lists of objects", but the reviewers can ask to reduce the scope in other cases too; if one out of two reviewers feels the complexity, then that's enough sign to reduce the scope.

I think we can reduce the scope of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121508. (cc @utam0k) 
I'll revisit all the other QHints (including pending PRs) later for this perspective. 

I'll defer the decision of DRA one to @pohly ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118893#issuecomment-2066524982)).

I also noticed that admin #121508  is too complex to maintain. Let me reduce the scope of #121508 . How can we decide the criterion for QHint scope?

Also, I have already created and submitted the PRs for QHint. I'd be happy if I could help with the reviews for PRs related to QHint.  If you assign me as the first reviewer, I may be able to comment on the sections that obviously need comment. This would surely reduce the review burden.

> If you assign me as the first reviewer, I may be able to comment on the sections that obviously need comment. This would surely reduce the review burden.

Thanks for stepping up. Always feel free to take the first passes. Unfortunately, we are rather limited on the time to get a second pass from approvers. And that's another reason to start with simple, smaller PRs.
That said, @sanposhiho has been doing tremendous work with reviews. Again, I'm trying to catch up, but I can't promise much yet.

Regarding DRA: I had already added one performance test for structured parameters earlier, about the common case with one claim per pod. `BenchmarkPerfScheduling/SchedulingWithResourceClaimTemplateStructured/2000pods_200nodes` improves a bit when enabling queuing hints (BTW, is it queuing or queueing?).

Average throughput increases by +14.89%, average scheduling duration goes down by -17.06%.

The less interesting from a real-world relevance perspective case is multiple pods sharing the same claim. I expect a higher impact of queuing hints there, but I need to work a bit on scheduler_perf before I can set up such a workload there.

`2000pods_200nodes`

I think problems only start to arise at 5k nodes with high churn (pods terminating and new pods incoming)

For "classic DRA" there was a significant slowdown when disabling queuing hints for `2000pods_200nodes`. I can re-run the structured parameters scenarios at higher pod and node counts.

OK, I look deeply into readWriteOncePodPVCsForPod.
We can ignore a deleted PVC associated with this deleted Pod because:
- if a new Pod has this PVC, this Pod won't be schedulable until the PVC with the same name is recreated.
- if a new Pod doesn't have this PVC, this Pod is completely not related to that deleted PVC.
